extracted.intended_audience: U.S. patent applicants, patent practitioners, and patent prosecutors
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for petitions to withdraw a holding of abandonment and for petitions to revive abandoned or lapsed U.S. patent applications under 37 CFR 1.137 (unavoidable/unintentional delay), including required contents, fees, and the standards of proof for delay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminal disclaimer condition for untimely petition to withdraw abandonment (post-June 8, 1995)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a petition to withdraw the holding of abandonment is untimely in a utility or plant application filed on or after June 8, 1995, the Office may treat the petition on its merits only if it is accompanied by a terminal disclaimer dedicating to the public a terminal part of the term of any patent granted that would extend beyond 20 years from the filing date (or earliest 35 U.S.C. 120/121/365(c) benefit).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The terminal disclaimer must also apply to any patent granted on any application that claims the benefit of the filing date under 35 U.S.C. 120, 121, or 365(c). Such a terminal disclaimer is required to avoid granting patent term extension under 35 U.S.C. 154(b) due to prosecution delay caused by treatment of the application as abandoned. (MPEP text)

rubrics_metrics.name: Dismissal for intentional delay
rubrics_metrics.description: If the record indicates that the applicant intentionally delayed filing a petition to withdraw the holding of abandonment, the Office may dismiss the petition as untimely (37 CFR 1.181(f)) solely on the basis of such intentional delay without addressing the merits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intentional delay in seeking revival precludes relief under 37 CFR 1.137(a) or (b). The Office may dismiss based on evidence of intentional delay without reaching merits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Showing required for petition to withdraw holding of abandonment based on nonreceipt of Office action
rubrics_metrics.description: An allegation that an Office action was never received may be considered if adequately supported; the showing must include a practitioner statement that the Office communication was not received and an attestation that a search of the file jacket and docket indicates nonreceipt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Must attach a copy of the docket record where the nonreceived communication would have been entered and reference it in the practitioner's statement (e.g., a docket report showing replies docketed for the date three months from the mail date if a three-month reply period was set). The Office may remail the Office action if the petition is granted (Delgar v. Schulyer reasoning). The outlined showing may be insufficient where circumstances suggest loss after receipt (e.g., practitioner has a history of not receiving Office actions). Nonreceipt of communications other than the action to which reply was required generally will not warrant withdrawal of the holding of abandonment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Available statutory/ regulatory bases to revive or accept late payments (scope of 37 CFR 1.137)
rubrics_metrics.description: 37 CFR 1.137 provides for revival of abandoned applications and lapsed patents for failure to: (A) timely reply to an Office requirement in a provisional application; (B) timely prosecute in a nonprovisional application; (C) timely pay the issue fee for a design application; (D) timely pay the issue fee for a utility or plant application; and (E) timely pay any outstanding balance of the issue fee (lapsed patents).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This enumerates the categories of situations in which petitions under 1.137 may be filed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirements for a petition under 37 CFR 1.137(a) (unavoidable delay)
rubrics_metrics.description: A petition under 37 CFR 1.137(a) must include: (A) the required reply, unless previously filed; (B) the petition fee as set forth in 37 CFR 1.17(l); (C) a showing to the satisfaction of the Commissioner that the entire delay in filing the required reply from its due date until filing of a grantable petition was unavoidable; and (D) any terminal disclaimer required pursuant to 37 CFR 1.137(d).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A showing of 'unavoidable' delay requires documentary evidence about procedures, training, and docketing records (see MPEP § 711.03(c)(III)(C)(2)). 37 CFR 1.137(a) is more exacting and petitions under it are less likely to be grantable as filed than under 1.137(b).

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirements for a petition under 37 CFR 1.137(b) (unintentional delay)
rubrics_metrics.description: A petition under 37 CFR 1.137(b) must include: (A) the required reply, unless previously filed; (B) the petition fee as set forth in 37 CFR 1.17(m); (C) a statement that the entire delay was unintentional; and (D) any terminal disclaimer required pursuant to 37 CFR 1.137(d).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commissioner may require additional information where there is a question whether the delay was unintentional. In the vast majority of 1.137(b) petitions the Office accepts the applicant's statement that 'the entire delay...was unintentional' without further evidence, relying upon the duty of candor (37 CFR 10.18). However, inappropriate statements can have adverse enforcement consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reply requirement — general
rubrics_metrics.description: A petition to revive under 37 CFR 1.137 must be accompanied by the required reply (i.e., the reply sufficient to have avoided abandonment if timely filed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In some circumstances the required reply may be met by filing a continuing application, RCE (for utility/plant apps filed on or after June 8, 1995), or payment of fees (issue/publication) as applicable. The Office has no authority to revive a case if no action was taken within the period for reply (Ex parte Richardson).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reply when abandonment was for failure to pay issue fee or publication fee
rubrics_metrics.description: For applications abandoned for failure to timely pay the issue fee, the required reply must include payment of the issue fee (or any outstanding balance). For abandonment for failure to pay the publication fee, the required reply must include payment of the publication fee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The filing of a continuing application without payment of the issue fee or outstanding balance is not an acceptable reply in an application abandoned for failure to pay the issue fee. If the Notice of Allowance required payment of a then-effective issue fee, payment of that fee (and any subsequent balance if fee increased) is necessary to revive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reply to a non-final action (nonprovisional applications)
rubrics_metrics.description: When abandonment resulted from failure to reply to a non-final action, the required reply may be either (A) an argument or amendment under 37 CFR 1.111; or (B) filing a continuing application under 37 CFR 1.53(b) (or a CPA under 1.53(d) in limited cases).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A petition may be granted if the proposed reply appears bona fide. After revival, an examiner may determine the reply is incomplete and issue a 1-month shortened statutory period under 37 CFR 1.135(c) to correct errors; if not corrected the application may again be abandoned. Extensions under 37 CFR 1.136(a) are permitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reply to a final action (nonprovisional applications)
rubrics_metrics.description: For abandonment due to failure to reply to a final action, the reply required for a petition to revive must comply with 37 CFR 1.113 and include cancellation of, or appeal from, the rejection of each claim so rejected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permissible replies include (A) a Notice of Appeal and appeal fee; (B) an amendment under 37 CFR 1.116 that cancels all rejected claims or otherwise prima facie places the application in condition for allowance; (C) filing an RCE (37 CFR 1.114) accompanied by a submission and fee for utility/plant apps (post-June 8,1995); or (D) filing a continuing application under 37 CFR 1.53(b) (or CPA under 1.53(d) in limited cases). If a proposed amendment is filed, the Office of Petitions may route it to the Technology Center to determine if the amendment places the application in condition for allowance; if not, the petition will not be granted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reply when abandonment was for failure to file an appeal brief
rubrics_metrics.description: If abandonment occurred because an appeal brief was not filed, the required reply under 37 CFR 1.137(a)(1) or 1.137(b)(1) must be either (A) an appeal brief in compliance with 37 CFR 1.192(c) and fee; (B) filing an RCE with a submission and fee (for utility/plant apps filed on/after June 8, 1995); or (C) filing a continuing application under 37 CFR 1.53(b) (or CPA under 1.53(d) in limited cases).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a notice of appeal is the reply filed, the Commissioner will set the time period under 37 CFR 1.192 for filing the appeal brief in the decision granting the petition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filing an RCE as the required reply — responsiveness requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: When an RCE is filed as the required reply to revive an application abandoned for failure to reply to a final action or to file an appeal brief, the submission accompanying the RCE must be a reply responsive within the meaning of 37 CFR 1.111 to the last Office action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Responsiveness is judged without factoring in the 'final' status of the action; the submission may be a previously filed amendment after final or incorporate by reference arguments in a previously filed appeal or reply brief. The petition may be granted if the submission appears to be a bona fide attempt to provide a complete reply. Examiner may later require corrections with a 1-month shortened statutory period (37 CFR 1.135(c)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Office may require a continuing application or RCE to meet the reply requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The Office may require filing a continuing application or an RCE to meet the reply requirement of 37 CFR 1.137(a)(1) or 1.137(b)(1) where treating a reply under 37 CFR 1.111 or 1.113 would place an inordinate burden on the Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exemplary circumstances include: (A) an application abandoned for an inordinate period of time; (B) application file contains multiple or conflicting replies to the last Office action; and (C) the reply or replies submitted under 37 CFR 1.137 are questionable as to compliance with 37 CFR 1.111 or 1.113.

rubrics_metrics.name: Petition fee requirement and nonrefundable status
rubrics_metrics.description: A petition to revive an unintentionally abandoned application (or unintentionally delayed payment) must be accompanied by the petition fee set forth in 37 CFR 1.17(m), unless filed under 35 U.S.C. 133 or 151 (unavoidable delay), in which case the fee is set forth in 37 CFR 1.17(l).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The fee is due on filing (not merely on grant). The Office will not refund the petition fee regardless of dismissal or denial, and will not reach the merits of any petition lacking the requisite fee.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between 'unintentional' and 'unavoidable' delay standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Petitions under 37 CFR 1.137(b) are evaluated under the less stringent 'unintentional' standard (statement(s) rather than documentary showing), whereas 37 CFR 1.137(a) requires proof that the delay was 'unavoidable' (more exacting showing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Office usually accepts statements under 1.137(b) because the applicant/practitioner has a duty of candor (37 CFR 10.18). A showing of unavoidable delay requires evidence about procedures in place, training and experience of responsible persons, and docketing records. Many petitions filed under 1.137(a) are ultimately granted under 1.137(b) when evidence for 'unavoidable' is difficult to obtain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences of inappropriate statements in 1.137(b) petitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Providing an inappropriate statement in a petition under 37 CFR 1.137(b) (e.g., falsely stating the delay was unintentional) may have adverse effects when attempting to enforce any patent resulting from the application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example case: Lumenyte Int’l Corp. v. Cable Lite Corp., where patents were held unenforceable due to inappropriate statements that abandonment was unintentional.

rubrics_metrics.name: What does not qualify as 'unintentional' or 'unavoidable' delay — deliberate decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: A delay resulting from a deliberately chosen course of action (e.g., applicant deliberately permits abandonment because claims are unpatentable, insufficient commercial value, to defer fees, or similar deliberate choices) is not 'unintentional' within 37 CFR 1.137(b) and precludes revival under either standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Change of mind after deliberate abandonment does not make the prior delay 'unintentional' (see In re Maldague, In re Application of G). Specific examples listed: (A) applicant does not consider claims patentable; (B) applicant considers allowed claims too narrow; (C) applicant considers patent not worth expense; (D) applicant not interested in obtaining patent; (E) applicant seeks to defer fees and expenses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard for 'unavoidable' delay — reasonably prudent person
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Unavoidable' delay is judged by the reasonably prudent person standard: requires no more care than generally used by prudent persons in important business, permitting reliance on ordinary/mail/telegraph, reliable employees, and usual instrumentalities; if failure occurs unexpectedly despite such precautions it may be unavoidable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decisions are case-by-case taking all facts and circumstances into account. Petitioner bears burden to establish delay was unavoidable; failure to do so precludes grant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Showing 'unavoidable' delay caused by clerical/employee error
rubrics_metrics.description: A delay resulting from an employee clerical error may support 'unavoidable' delay if: (A) the error caused the delay; (B) there was a business routine in place reasonably relied upon to avoid such errors; and (C) the employee was sufficiently trained and experienced with regard to the function and routine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited cases: In re Egbers, In re Katrapat. Examples include change of correspondence address leading to mailing to old address — an adequate showing requires evidence that due care was taken to notify the Office in a manner reasonably calculated to call attention to the change (see MPEP § 601.03).

rubrics_metrics.name: What does not constitute proper notification of change of correspondence address
rubrics_metrics.description: The following do NOT constitute proper notification of a change in correspondence address: (A) mere inclusion of a different address in a paper filed for another purpose without mention of an address change; (B) notification on a paper listing plural applications as affected (except under Customer Number practice); or (C) lack of notification or belated notification to the USPTO of the change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proper, timely, and conspicuous notification is required to support claims of unavoidable delay due to address changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delays due to lack of knowledge or improper application of statute/rules/MPEP are not 'unavoidable'
rubrics_metrics.description: Delay resulting from lack of knowledge or improper application of the patent statute, rules of practice, or the MPEP does not constitute 'unavoidable' delay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reliance on oral advice from USPTO employees or the USPTO's failure to advise in sufficient time does not render such delays unavoidable (cases cited: Haines v. Quigg; Vincent v. Mossinghoff; Smith v. Diamond; Potter v. Dann; In re Sivertz). Also, failure to file papers/fees in compliance with 37 CFR 1.8 or 1.10 does not constitute unavoidable delay.
